answers.justification: C5 shows the same claim rate for new and legacy installers on Pellacott 2026 valves (42 vs 41) and 5–7 per 1,000 for Durrant-Hale valves in every installer group; brazed joints were intact and never-installed warehouse valves leak at the seat (C5). C1 shows the new installers had clean audits, so E5/C6 reflect the build-year confound.

C10 found LT-04 out of service since 9 Jan 2026, no VA-220 program on any other rig and per-piece tables copied from four 2025 sequences, yet E6/C4 certify 2026 lots on LT-04; C5 shows 11% of never-installed 2026 Pellacott valves leak, against 1% for 2025-built and 0% for Durrant-Hale.
C10 shows the certified rig LT-04 was disconnected for all of 2026, no other rig could test the VA-220 and the result tables repeat earlier sequences, so the recorded tests were not performed.

C5 shows firmware 4.1 and 4.2 units fail at similar rates (40 vs 42) and Durrant-Hale valves are unaffected; E2 shows the rise began with January builds, before the 10 Mar rollout (C2), and warehouse valves that were never powered still leak (C5).
C8 shows a programme-wide jump in test-record conformance and no collection of rig logs, so the weakness exists, but no evidence checks whether any other supplier's records are fabricated.

The defect appears in never-installed, never-powered warehouse valves (C5: 11% vs 1% and 0%), teardown shows seat leakage matching the main claim code (C5, E2), the timing fits the January change (E4, E2), and the claim breakdown rules out installer and firmware rivals (C5).
In C5, valve source rather than installer group drives claims: 41 vs 42 for Pellacott valves and 5–7 for Durrant-Hale valves across all installer groups.
C5 shows no firmware difference (40 vs 42) and low Durrant-Hale rates on both versions, and E2 shows the rise started before the March rollout (C2).

Deformed slide seals (C5) and untested compression set (C11) fit a seal cause, but C5 states every 2026 sample has both the Corlin seal and Line 3 assembly, so the seal change cannot be separated from the line move.

By the formula in E3, test-record conformance (weight 0.40) going from 58 to 100 accounts for most of the 70→89 rise while the audit and delivery components barely moved; C13 confirms the paperwork drove dock-to-stock.

C10 shows the certificates are untrustworthy and C5 shows 11% of 2026 Pellacott stock leaks before installation, so quarantine plus independent helium testing (C5 method) protects the field without losing usable stock.
C5 and C1 clear the new installers, so suspending them and charging claims back would punish the wrong party.
Fresh certificates (C4, E1) would come from the same fabricated process (C10), and 2026 lots have an 11% seat-leak rate (C5); releasing them on paperwork would ship known-suspect valves.
The seal is a plausible cause (C5, C11), but it is confounded with the Line 3 move and the compound has not been analysed (C5), so mandating Ferrand now is not justified.

C8, C13 and C3 show SupplierPath rewards unverified paperwork across 15 dock-to-stock suppliers, so requiring rig logs or witnessed tests is sound, but waiting for the next cycle leaves existing dock-to-stock grants unchecked, so it is reasonable rather than the top action.
C10, C5 (warehouse retest and claim breakdown) and E2 together justify committing to A1 now; A1 includes verification testing, so it does not depend on settling the seal-versus-line question.

ambiguousItems: I10: 'causal' rests on the score formula (E3), but the conformance component may measure how complete the records are rather than the 100% pass rates themselves, so 'association-only' is also defensible.

I15: A5 fixes the systemic weakness shown in C8/C13 and could be judged 'preferred'; I rated it 'acceptable' because it only takes effect from the next audit cycle and leaves the 15 existing dock-to-stock grants in place.
I9: 'association-only' versus 'unknown' depends on whether the Corlin/Line 3 confound counts as association or as insufficient evidence.
caseProblems: C10's title ('independent-observation', calibration contractor report on the leak-test rigs) and C5's title (claim breakdown) point strongly toward the key evidence, but they do not state the answer.
C5 is dated 30 Oct 2026, after the COO's 12 Oct request in E1, but it is still labelled stage S1; this is a minor timeline inconsistency.
The H3 vs H2 split is settled entirely by C10; without C10, H3 would be undecidable because Pellacott's test method was not replicated (C5).

rulings.explanation: The key's 'causal' rests on E3's formula: the 0.40-weighted test-record conformance component rose from 58 to 100 and accounts for about 17 of the 19 points. But R5's cause node is specifically the '100% pass rates' in the records, and the evidence never says the conformance component scores pass rates. The only concrete information about what it measures points to completeness: the 58 baseline is explained as 'per-piece leak values missing on 9 of 14 certificates'. C13 ('worst paperwork to our best... full per-piece tables on every lot') and C3 ('complete, all lots 100% pass') do not separate completeness from pass rate either. So it is mechanically established that the submitted records drove the score rise. It is not established that the 100% pass feature did, as opposed to the records simply being complete. A careful analyst could therefore say the 100% pass rates only co-occurred with the score rise ('association-only'). Calling the link 'causal' requires assuming that conformance includes passing against the limit. Both answers can be defended.
rulings.fix: Add a definition to E3 that makes pass rate part of the component, e.g. 'Test-record conformance = percentage of lot certificates that have complete per-piece values with every piece within the leak limit.' With that, 'causal' is the only defensible answer. Alternatively, reword R5's cause node to 'Pellacott's complete, all-pass submitted test records' so it matches what E3 shows drove the component.

rulings.explanation: A5 is not premature: the scoring weakness is confirmed. E3 shows that unverified self-reported records drove the score and automatically granted dock-to-stock, and C10 shows those records were fabricated. A5 is not harmful either. The question is whether it is 'preferred' or 'acceptable'. The case writes two limits into A5 on purpose. First, it takes effect only 'from the next audit cycle'. Second, it does nothing about the current risk: the defective 2026 Pellacott stock, the held lots, and, per C8, the 15 dock-to-stock grants already issued on the same unverified records while H5 remains open. A careful analyst would see that a better action is available now: immediate containment (A1), plus, systemically, suspending or re-verifying the existing grants. A5 delays even the systemic fix, so it is a reasonable but not best-in-class next action. It is better than A2, A3 and A4, but 'preferred' means among the best next actions given the evidence, not merely the best of the listed options. The deferred start and the untouched existing grants push it below that bar. 'Acceptable' is the defensible answer.
rulings.fix: No change needed. Optionally, to make the point even clearer, add to the key's rationale that A5 leaves C8's 15 existing unverified dock-to-stock grants in place until the next cycle.

rulings.explanation: Under the stated semantics, 'unknown' means the evidence is insufficient even to show association. Association between the Corlin seal and seat leakage is clearly shown. Every 2026-built Pellacott valve has the Corlin seal (E4, C5), and these leak at the seat at 11% in never-installed stock, against 1% for 2025-built valves with the Ferrand seal and 0% for Durrant-Hale. In 38 of 41 teardowns the defect is in the slide seal itself, which is deformed and unseated. Causation is not established. C5 states that the seal compound was not analysed and that the seal is fully confounded with the Line 3 assembly change, and C11 shows that compression set and oil compatibility were never tested on production lots. A confound blocks a causal conclusion; it does not remove the co-occurrence. So the Corlin/Line 3 confound is exactly what makes the answer 'association-only' rather than 'unknown'. 'Causal' is also excluded, because the main rival (Line 3 assembly) is not ruled out.
